title: The website nobody could see inside
teaches: What "working" means (SLIs, SLOs, error budgets), the four golden signals, alerting on symptoms, and storing metrics

blocks.text: On Tuesday 1 October 2013 the United States government opened HealthCare.gov, where people in most states could compare health insurance plans and sign up for one under the new Affordable Care Act. Millions of people tried on the first day. Pages hung, accounts could not be created, and the step that checked people's identities often failed. Notes from the first days, later made public by Congress and reported in the press, put the number who completed enrolment on the first day in single figures.

In the middle of October a small group was brought in to help, under the administration's chief technology officer, Todd Park, and later Jeff Zients, who was put in charge of the repair. Among them was Mikey Dickerson, an engineer who took leave from Google's site reliability team. What they found surprised them more than the bugs. Dozens of contractors had built the parts of the site, and there was no single place where anyone could see whether it was working: how many people were trying to sign up, how many succeeded, how long pages took, or which part was failing. Teams argued from their own logs and their own impressions. One of the first things the rescue team did was install monitoring across the whole system, put its numbers on a screen everyone could see, and hold a daily meeting around them.[^usds]

With the numbers visible, the team could rank problems by how many people each one affected and fix them in that order. By the start of December the site worked for most people who used it. The rescuers realized that the core problem was not any single bug: you cannot systematically fix a system that nobody can measure. In this lesson, we will define what "working" means in numbers, watch those numbers, configure alerts to wake engineers only when user-facing problems occur, and store those metrics cheaply enough to keep.

Google had been running production this way for a decade by then; its 2016 book *Site Reliability Engineering* set out the vocabulary most teams now use. A **service level indicator**, an SLI, is a measured ratio of good events divided by all valid events. Valid leaves out what the service should not be blamed for, such as requests refused for bad input, health checks and test traffic. At scale nobody computes it from raw logs at query time. Instead, each load balancer keeps two counters a minute, valid and good, and the monitoring system takes the ratio from the sums. "Share of requests answered without a server error" is one SLI. "Share of requests answered in under 300 ms" is another, and stating a latency goal as a share of requests is better than using an average, because, as we saw in lesson 9, an average hides the high-latency tail that users experience.

A **service level objective**, an SLO, is a target for an SLI over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over the last 30 days. A **service level agreement**, an SLA, is a promise in a contract, with financial penalties if it is broken; it is usually looser than the SLO, so the engineering team notices trouble before the lawyers do.

An engineer's first instinct is often to set a target of 100%, which is a mistake. No service reaches 100%, so the first minor failure breaks the target, and the team learns to ignore it. Users cannot tell 99.99% from 100% anyway, because their own mobile networks and Wi-Fi fail more often than that. Engineers name targets by their **nines**: 99.9% is three nines, and 99.99% is four nines. By a common rule of thumb, each extra nine costs about ten times as much as the one before in spare machines, slower releases and on-call staffing. You should set the target to the lowest level that users, measured from their perspective, would call working.

blocks.caption: How long a service may fail completely in 30 days and still meet its target. Each extra nine divides the allowance by ten.

blocks.text: Before choosing indicators, ask what users of the service are trying to do. For a website, users want pages that load and actions that complete. For a storage system, they want reads that return the right bytes and writes that are not lost. For a data pipeline, they want fresh output, such as the share of hours in which yesterday's numbers were ready by 9 a.m. You should measure as close to the user as possible. A server's own logs miss the requests that never reached it, whereas the load balancer's logs, or an external probe, will capture them.

The complement of the SLO is the **error budget**. A 99.9% target over 30 days allows 0.1% of requests to fail: about 43 minutes of complete outage, or three days of one request in a hundred failing, or a whole month of one in a thousand failing, or any mix of these. The budget turns a recurring dispute between teams into arithmetic. Developers want to ship changes, while operators want nothing to change. With an error budget, both sides agree in advance that while budget remains, the team can ship features; when the budget is spent, the team stops shipping features and works on reliability until the budget recovers.

The budget also tells you when to wake someone up. The **burn rate** is how fast the service consumes the budget, compared with spending it evenly over the window. At a burn rate of 1, the budget lasts the full 30 days; at a burn rate of 14.4, the whole month's budget is gone in 50 hours. Google's follow-up book, *The Site Reliability Workbook* (2018), suggests paging an engineer when 2% of the month's budget is spent in an hour (a burn rate of 14.4) or 5% in six hours (a burn rate of 6), and opening a ticket when 10% is spent in three days (a burn rate of 1). Each rule also checks a shorter window, one-twelfth as long (such as five minutes alongside the one-hour window), and fires only when both windows exceed the threshold. The long window prevents a brief spike from paging anyone, while the short window resets the alert soon after the outage ends. High burn rates page an engineer immediately, while low burn rates open a ticket for the next workday.

blocks.caption: A month of one service against its target, played day by day: the error budget left, the hours with failing requests, and when alerts on burn rate and on CPU would have paged someone. The month's events are made up; the alert rules are from the workbook.
blocks.task: Guess, then play the month to the end

blocks.text: The two alert rows illustrate the difference between paging on causes and paging on symptoms. The CPU alert fires every night once a batch job starts filling the machines in the early hours. The batch job never affects a user, and the two CPU alerts that happen to fall during the slow leak are unrelated to it. A team paged twenty times a month for false alarms learns to ignore the pager, and then misses a real outage. The burn-rate alerts fire only when user requests are failing. That includes the slow leak, where a dependency fails 0.4% of calls for two and a half days starting on day 14; a static threshold on the per-minute error rate would miss this because a 0.4% error rate rarely looks alarming in a single minute. Against a 99.9% target, a 0.4% error rate is a burn rate of 4, which does not page anyone but opens a ticket within the first day. If you raise the target to 99.99%, the baseline background rate of one failure in five thousand (0.02%) is already twice what the budget allows, so the alert never stops firing. Setting a target tighter than the system can meet only produces alert noise.

The general rule is to **alert on symptoms, not causes**. A symptom is something users experience, such as errors, high latency or stale data. A cause is a potential reason for a symptom, such as high CPU utilisation, a full disk or a restarted process. Causes belong on dashboards, where an engineer diagnosing a symptom can inspect them. A page should mean that a person must act immediately, and you should fix or delete any paging alert that does not require action.

The SRE book defines **four golden signals** to monitor for every request-serving system. **Latency** is the time it takes to serve a request, tracking failed requests separately from successful ones, since a fast error is not a fast success. **Traffic** is the demand placed on the system, measured in requests a second or another rate suited to the service. **Errors** are the rate of requests that fail, either explicitly (such as HTTP 500s) or implicitly (returning a 200 OK with the wrong content). **Saturation** is how close the service is to full capacity, measured by the most constrained resource, such as threads, memory, queue depth or disk I/O. As we saw in lesson 2, saturation degrades performance well before utilisation reaches 100%, because queueing delay climbs steeply as a resource approaches capacity.

Aggregating latency across machines requires care. Each server can compute its own 99th percentile latency, but you cannot average percentiles: the mean of fifty servers' p99 values is not the fleet's p99, and can differ from it significantly. Instead, servers record request latencies into a **histogram** of fixed buckets, such as under 10 ms, 10 to 25 ms, 25 to 50 ms, and so on. Your monitoring system can sum the bucket counts across servers and across minutes, and then estimate any percentile from the combined histogram to the precision of the bucket boundaries. You should place one bucket boundary exactly at the SLO's latency threshold, so that the share of requests under 300 ms is exact, and space the remaining bucket boundaries exponentially (each roughly twice as wide as the last).[^hist]

Every metric is stored as a **time series**: a metric name, a set of key-value labels, and a sequence of timestamped values. A request counter labelled with service `checkout`, status `500` and region `us-east` is one time series; each distinct combination of label values creates another series. The total number of series, known as the **cardinality**, is the primary scaling bottleneck for monitoring systems. Consider the numbers before we design the store: 50 services, 10 endpoints per service, 5 HTTP status classes and 4 regions produce 50 × 10 × 5 × 4 = 10,000 time series for a single metric. If you add a label for customer ID across a million customers, that one metric expands to ten billion series. Labels with unbounded values belong in logs and traces, not in time-series metrics.

A large company collects millions of time series, sampling each one roughly every 10 seconds. Stored uncompressed, each data point takes 16 bytes: a 64-bit integer timestamp and a 64-bit floating-point value. In 2015, Facebook engineers Tuomas Pelkonen and colleagues published Gorilla, an in-memory time-series database that held the most recent 26 hours of Facebook's monitoring data in front of a slower disk-backed store (HBase). Gorilla's compression algorithm is now standard across monitoring systems, including Prometheus. It relies on two properties of real monitoring data. First, samples arrive at nearly constant intervals, so the difference between consecutive intervals is usually zero. Second, consecutive values are often identical or nearly identical, so the bitwise XOR of a value with its predecessor (which outputs 1 only where bits differ) is either all zeros or contains a short run of non-zero bits.

blocks.caption: A minute of one server's request rate, encoded the Gorilla way. A repeated value or an unchanged gap costs a single bit; a change costs a few more.

blocks.text: Gorilla stores the change in the gap between timestamps, called the **delta-of-delta**: zero costs one bit, a change of up to 64 seconds either way costs 9 bits (a 2-bit prefix and 7 bits of value), and up to 256 seconds 12 bits. A value equal to the last costs one bit. A different one costs two control bits and the XOR's **meaningful bits**, the run between its leading and trailing zeros; when that run is wider than the last one's, 11 more bits say where it starts and how long it is. Nothing is rounded: every point can be read back exactly. Across Facebook's data the paper reports about 1.37 bytes a point, a twelfth of the plain 16. **An estimate** of what that buys: 10 million series at a point every 10 s is a million points a second. Over 26 hours that is 94 billion points: 1.5 TB stored plainly, about 130 GB compressed, which fits in the memory of a handful of machines.[^gorilla]

Designing a metric store at this scale involves three further architectural choices. First, **pull versus push**: Prometheus (started at SoundCloud in 2012) pulls metrics by scraping each server over HTTP, which lets the collector detect immediately when a target server stops responding, whereas pushing metrics suits short-lived batch jobs that might exit before a scraper polls them. Second, **retention and downsampling**: systems keep recent data at full 10-second resolution and downsample older data to 1-minute or 1-hour rollups, just as Gorilla kept 26 hours in RAM and wrote older data to disk. Third, **regional hierarchy**: Google's Monarch (2020) stores each region's metrics inside that region, keeping ingestion local and isolated from outages in other regions, and answers global queries by fanning out sub-queries to every region and merging the results (the scatter-gather pattern from lesson 9). Finally, because a monitoring system must remain up when production is down, it should share as few dependencies with production services as possible, following the same isolation principle as the status page in lesson 23.

blocks.title: From the user back to the store
points: Decide what users call working, and state it as a share of good events over a window.
Spend the error budget on change, and alert when it burns fast.
Page on symptoms; keep causes on dashboards.
Count latency into histograms; never average percentiles.
Watch cardinality: every label value multiplies the series.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on SLOs and monitoring
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A service has an availability SLO of 99.9% over 30 days. About how many minutes of complete outage does its error budget allow?
choices: About 43 minutes
About 4 minutes
About 7 hours
items.why: 0.1% of 30 days (43,200 minutes) is 43.2 minutes. A 99.99% target allows 4.32 minutes, and a 99% target allows 7.2 hours.

items.ask: Which is the best indicator for a web checkout's latency?
choices: The share of checkout requests answered in under 500 ms, measured by each checkout server
The mean checkout response time, measured at the load balancer, held under 500 ms
The share of checkout requests answered in under 500 ms, measured at the load balancer
items.why: A share of good requests is an SLI that can be summed and given a target, and the load balancer also sees requests that never reached a server or crashed it. A mean hides the high-latency tail.

items.ask: A team pages its on-call engineer whenever CPU stays above 90% for ten minutes. Why is that a poor alert?
choices: CPU is measured too coarsely on modern servers to be a reliable number to alert on
High CPU is a possible cause, not a symptom: it fires while users are fine and misses real failures
Ten minutes is too short a window, so the alert fires on every brief spike in load and wakes people needlessly
items.why: Users experience errors and high latency, not CPU utilisation. Alerts on causes page people when users are unaffected and miss failures caused by other issues, so pages should trigger on symptoms such as high error-budget burn rates.

items.ask: A service is failing 0.5% of requests, steadily, against a 99.9% SLO over 30 days. What is its burn rate, and what do the workbook's rules do?
choices: 5: the budget would last about six days; the six-hour rule pages someone at once
5: the budget would last about six days; a ticket is opened, but nobody is paged
0.5: half the budget is being spent, so no alert fires and it can carry on
items.why: The budget allows a 0.1% failure rate, so a 0.5% failure rate consumes the budget five times faster than an even pace. Paging requires a burn rate of 6 over six hours or 14.4 over one hour; spending 10% in three days (a burn rate of 1) opens a ticket.

items.ask: Why is a 100% availability target a mistake for almost any service?
choices: Monitoring systems cannot measure availability precisely enough to confirm a service has reached 100%
Contracts with customers forbid promising 100%, so the SLO would conflict with the SLA
It cannot be met, so it is broken at once and ignored, and users can't tell it from 99.99%
items.why: A target that leaves no error budget gives no room for shipping changes and produces noisy alerts, and every extra nine costs much more for a difference that users' own network connections hide.

items.ask: Someone proposes adding a user_id label to a request-count metric that has 10,000 series, for a service with two million users. What happens?
choices: The metric can grow toward 20 billion series, far beyond what the store can hold
The metric doubles in size, since each request now carries one more label
Nothing much, because a time-series store compresses repeated labels to almost nothing
items.why: Each distinct combination of label values creates its own time series, so the cardinality multiplies: 10,000 × 2 million. Per-user detail belongs in logs or traces.

items.ask: Why does Gorilla's compression bring a typical monitoring point from 16 bytes to under 2 bytes?
choices: It stores each value at lower precision, rounding it to the nearest whole number, and packs each timestamp into one byte
It keeps only the points that differ from the previous one and drops the rest entirely
Regular readings change little, so the change in gap and the XOR with the last value are mostly zeros
items.why: Delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-ed floating-point values compress an unchanged interval and an unchanged value to a single bit each, without rounding: every point is reconstructed exactly.

summary: **You cannot fix what you cannot measure.** One of the first things HealthCare.gov's rescuers did was install monitoring and put its metrics on a screen where everyone could see them.
**An SLI is the ratio of good events to valid events.** State latency as the share of requests faster than a threshold, measured as close to users as possible.
**An SLO is a target over a time window, and never 100%.** By a common rule of thumb, each extra nine costs about ten times as much as the last, for a difference users may not notice.

**The error budget is the unreliability the SLO allows.** A 99.9% target over 30 days gives 43 minutes of total outage; spend that budget on shipping changes, and freeze feature releases when it runs out.
**Alert on burn rate.** Page an engineer when the budget burns fast, open a ticket when it burns slowly, and keep underlying causes such as CPU utilisation on dashboards.
**Watch the four golden signals.** Track latency, traffic, errors and saturation for every request-serving system.
**Percentiles cannot be averaged.** Record latencies into histogram buckets, whose counts can be summed across servers and time windows.
**Cardinality drives the cost of a metric.** Every distinct combination of label values creates a time series, so unbounded labels such as user IDs belong in logs, not metrics.
**Gorilla compresses a data point to about 1.37 bytes.** Delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-encoded values represent an unchanged interval or value in a single bit.

usds.title: What came after
usds.text: Several of the rescuers stayed on. In August 2014 the White House founded the United States Digital Service, with Dickerson as its first administrator, to bring engineers into government on short tours to work on systems like HealthCare.gov.

hist.title: Sketches for percentiles
hist.text: Fixed buckets give percentiles only as fine as the buckets. Structures such as t-digest and DDSketch adapt their buckets to the data so that any percentile comes out within a set relative error, and they still merge across servers.

gorilla.title: Where the ratio comes from
gorilla.text: Most series in Gorilla's data changed rarely or slowly; a value that never changes costs two bits a point when sampled on a regular clock. Values that fluctuate rapidly compress far less, and the 1.37-byte figure is an average across Facebook's production metrics.
